hooks.text: No nation can ever own the Moon.
Who actually owns the Moon under international space law?
118 countries signed a treaty banning nuclear weapons in space.

title: The Cold War Treaty That Banned Nuclear Weapons in Space
description: Discover the 1967 Outer Space Treaty that banned nuclear weapons in orbit and kept the Moon free of sovereign claims.

beats.text: No nation can ever own the Moon.
beats.visual: Apollo 11 astronaut Buzz Aldrin on the Moon, 1969

beats.text: During the intense geopolitical tensions of the Cold War, the United States and the Soviet Union faced a dangerous new frontier.
beats.visual: Atlas ICBM rocket test launch from the late 1950s

beats.text: On January 27, 1967, rival superpowers opened the Outer Space Treaty for signature in Washington, London, and Moscow.
beats.visual: Signing of the Outer Space Treaty in Washington, D.C. in 1967
queries: Signing of the Outer Space Treaty Washington

beats.text: This foundational agreement strictly bans countries from placing nuclear weapons or weapons of mass destruction in Earth orbit.
The treaty explicitly forbids claiming sovereignty over any celestial body and legally designates outer space as the province of all mankind.
beats.visual: Neil Armstrong next to the US flag on the Moon, 1969

beats.text: Yet remarkably, the treaty does not explicitly ban conventional military weapons in space.
beats.visual: Artist concept of commercial asteroid mining operations, 2020

beats.text: This Cold War relic keeps the heavens peaceful because no nation can ever own the Moon.
beats.visual: Earth rising over the lunar horizon, Apollo 8, 1968
